root_theorem.statement_nl: For $n \geq 2$, let $A = [a_{i,j}]_{i,j=1}^n$ be an $n$-by-$n$ matrix of nonnegative integers such that (a) $a_{i,j} = 0$ when $i+j\leq n$; (b) $a_{i+1,j} \in \{a_{i,j}, a_{i,j}+1\}$ when $1 \leq i \leq n-1$ and $1 \leq j \leq n$; and (c) $a_{i,j+1} \in \{a_{i,j}, a_{i,j}+1\}$ when $1 \leq i \leq n$ and $1 \leq j \leq n-1$. Let $S$ be the sum of the entries of $A$, and let $N$ be the number of nonzero entries of $A$. Prove that \[ S \leq \frac{(n+2)N}{3}. \]

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n >= 2 and every n x n matrix A = [a_{i,j}] with entries in Z_{>=0}, if (i) a_{i,j} = 0 for every 1 <= i,j <= n with i+j <= n, (ii) for every 1 <= i <= n-1 and 1 <= j <= n one has a_{i+1,j} - a_{i,j} in {0,1}, and (iii) for every 1 <= i <= n and 1 <= j <= n-1 one has a_{i,j+1} - a_{i,j} in {0,1}, then with S = sum_{i=1}^n sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j} and N = #{(i,j) in [1,n]^2 : a_{i,j} > 0}, the inequality 3S <= (n+2)N holds.

selected_decomposition.strategy_summary: Use the support E = {(i,j) : a_{i,j} > 0} as a southeast-closed Ferrers diagram. For each positive cell, bound its value simultaneously by three easier quantities: its horizontal positive rank in its row, its vertical positive rank in its column, and its distance from the zero anti-diagonal. Summing the pointwise inequality 3a_{i,j} <= x_{i,j} + y_{i,j} + z_{i,j} reduces the theorem to three explicit combinatorial summation formulas over the Ferrers diagram, whose total is exactly (n+2)N.

steps.derives: Let E = {(i,j) : a_{i,j} > 0}. For each i, define l_i = #{j : a_{i,j} > 0}. Then E = {(i,j) : n-l_i+1 <= j <= n}, the sequence l_1,...,l_n is weakly increasing with l_i <= i, and N = sum_{i=1}^n l_i.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of L1.

steps.derives: For each (i,j) in E, define x_{i,j} = #{k <= j : a_{i,k} > 0}, y_{i,j} = #{k <= i : a_{k,j} > 0}, and z_{i,j} = i+j-n. Then a_{i,j} <= x_{i,j}, a_{i,j} <= y_{i,j}, and a_{i,j} <= z_{i,j}, hence 3a_{i,j} <= x_{i,j} + y_{i,j} + z_{i,j}. Summing over (i,j) in E gives 3S <= X + Y + Z, where X = sum_{(i,j) in E} x_{i,j}, Y = sum_{(i,j) in E} y_{i,j}, and Z = sum_{(i,j) in E} z_{i,j}.
steps.trivial_justification: Each of the three inequalities is provided by L2, L3, and L4, and summing them over the positive support E gives the displayed bound because S = sum_{(i,j) in E} a_{i,j}.
Apply L5 to the Ferrers shape E described in A1.
By L6, Y equals sum_k mu_k(mu_k+1)/2 for the column heights mu_k of E; by L7 this equals sum_i (n+1-i)l_i.
Apply L8 to the same Ferrers shape E from A1.
This is immediate algebra, using N = sum_i l_i from A1.

steps.derives: From 3S <= X + Y + Z and X + Y + Z = (n+2)N, we get 3S <= (n+2)N, hence S <= ((n+2)N)/3.
steps.trivial_justification: Substitution followed by division by 3 yields exactly the root theorem.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Encode the positive support as a southeast-closed Ferrers diagram with row lengths l_i. For each positive cell, bound its value by three quantities: horizontal positive rank, vertical positive rank, and distance from the zero anti-diagonal. Summing these three bounds gives 3S <= X+Y+Z. The three pure combinatorial lemmas compute X, Y, and Z explicitly in terms of the l_i, and those expressions add up to (n+2)N.

lemmas.statement_nl: For every integer n >= 2 and every n x n matrix A = [a_{i,j}] with entries in Z_{>=0} such that (i) a_{i,j} = 0 whenever 1 <= i,j <= n and i+j <= n, (ii) a_{i+1,j} - a_{i,j} is in {0,1} whenever 1 <= i <= n-1 and 1 <= j <= n, and (iii) a_{i,j+1} - a_{i,j} is in {0,1} whenever 1 <= i <= n and 1 <= j <= n-1, define E = {(i,j) : 1 <= i,j <= n and a_{i,j} > 0}. Then E is southeast-closed in the sense that if (i,j) is in E and i <= i' <= n and j <= j' <= n, then (i',j') is in E. Also, for each row index i define l_i = # {j in {1,...,n} : a_{i,j} > 0}. Then 0 <= l_i <= i for every i, one has l_1 <= l_2 <= ... <= l_n, and E is exactly the set of pairs (i,j) with 1 <= i <= n and n-l_i+1 <= j <= n. Consequently, if N = #E, then N = sum_{i=1}^n l_i.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer n >= 2 and every matrix A = (a_{i,j})_{1<=i,j<=n} with entries in Z_{>=0} satisfying: (1) a_{i,j}=0 for all 1<=i,j<=n with i+j<=n; (2) a_{i+1,j}-a_{i,j} is either 0 or 1 for all 1<=i<=n-1, 1<=j<=n; and (3) a_{i,j+1}-a_{i,j} is either 0 or 1 for all 1<=i<=n, 1<=j<=n-1; define E={(i,j):1<=i,j<=n and a_{i,j}>0}. Then E is southeast-closed: whenever (i,j) is in E and i<=i'<=n and j<=j'<=n, one has (i',j') in E. For each row i in {1,...,n}, let l_i be the number of columns j with a_{i,j}>0. Then for every i, 0<=l_i<=i; the sequence (l_i) is nondecreasing, i.e. l_1<=l_2<=...<=l_n; and E is exactly the union over rows i of the rightmost l_i positions in that row, equivalently (i,j) in E iff 1<=i<=n and n-l_i+1<=j<=n. Therefore, if N=|E|, then N equals the row-sum count sum_{i=1}^n l_i.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix n >= 2 and a matrix A = [a_{i,j}]_{i,j=1}^n satisfying the three stated conditions, and define E = {(i,j) : a_{i,j} > 0}. For each row i, let P_i := {j in {1,...,n} : a_{i,j} > 0}, so l_i = |P_i|.

First we record the monotonicity forced by (ii) and (iii).

If 1 <= i <= n and j <= j' <= n, then
a_{i,j'} - a_{i,j} = sum_{t=j}^{j'-1} (a_{i,t+1} - a_{i,t}).
Each summand belongs to {0,1} by (iii), hence is >= 0. Therefore a_{i,j'} >= a_{i,j}.
Similarly, if 1 <= j <= n and i <= i' <= n, then
a_{i',j} - a_{i,j} = sum_{s=i}^{i'-1} (a_{s+1,j} - a_{s,j}),
whose summands are all in {0,1} by (ii), so again a_{i',j} >= a_{i,j}.

Now let (i,j) be in E, so a_{i,j} > 0, and suppose i <= i' <= n and j <= j' <= n. By the row monotonicity just proved, a_{i,j'} >= a_{i,j} > 0. Then by the column monotonicity, a_{i',j'} >= a_{i,j'} > 0. Hence (i',j') is in E. This proves that E is southeast-closed.

Next we prove 0 <= l_i <= i for each i.
The lower bound l_i >= 0 is immediate because l_i is a cardinality. For the upper bound, if j <= n-i, then i+j <= n, so by condition (i) we have a_{i,j} = 0. Thus any positive entry in row i must lie in one of the columns n-i+1, n-i+2, ..., n, of which there are exactly i. Hence l_i <= i.

We now show l_1 <= l_2 <= ... <= l_n. Let 1 <= i <= n-1. If j is in P_i, then (i,j) is in E. By southeast-closure, taking i' = i+1 and j' = j, we get (i+1,j) in E, so j is in P_{i+1}. Therefore P_i subseteq P_{i+1}, and taking cardinalities gives l_i <= l_{i+1}. This holds for every i = 1,...,n-1, so the whole sequence is nondecreasing.

Now fix a row i. Because E is southeast-closed, if j is in P_i and j <= j' <= n, then (i,j') is also in E; equivalently j' is in P_i. So P_i is a suffix of {1,...,n}.

If l_i = 0, then P_i is empty, and the interval condition n-l_i+1 <= j <= n becomes n+1 <= j <= n, which describes the empty set. Thus in this case P_i = {j : n-l_i+1 <= j <= n}.

If l_i > 0, let m_i be the smallest element of P_i. Since P_i is a suffix, we have P_i = {m_i, m_i+1, ..., n}. Therefore
l_i = |P_i| = n - m_i + 1,
so m_i = n - l_i + 1. Hence
P_i = {n-l_i+1, n-l_i+2, ..., n} = {j : n-l_i+1 <= j <= n}.

So for every i,
P_i = {j in {1,...,n} : n-l_i+1 <= j <= n}.
Equivalently,
(i,j) is in E if and only if 1 <= i <= n and n-l_i+1 <= j <= n.
This is exactly the claimed description of E.

Finally, since E is the disjoint union of the row sets {(i,j) : j in P_i} for i = 1,...,n, we have
N = |E| = sum_{i=1}^n |P_i| = sum_{i=1}^n l_i.

All required statements follow.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix n, A, i, j satisfying the hypotheses, and assume a_{i,j}>0. Define
T := {k in {1,...,j} : a_{i,k}>0}.
Then j belongs to T, so T is nonempty. Let t := min T.

First, the entries in row i are nondecreasing as the column index increases: for every k with 1<=k<=n-1, hypothesis (iii) says a_{i,k+1}-a_{i,k} is in {0,1}, hence a_{i,k+1}>=a_{i,k}. Therefore, since a_{i,t}>0, we have a_{i,k}>=a_{i,t}>0 for every k with t<=k<=j. By minimality of t, no index < t lies in T. Hence
T = {t,t+1,...,j},
so
x_{i,j} = |T| = j-t+1.

Next I claim that a_{i,t}=1.

Case 1: t>1. Since t is the first positive index in row i up to column j, we have a_{i,t-1}=0. Applying hypothesis (iii) at (i,t-1),
a_{i,t}-a_{i,t-1} is in {0,1}.
Because a_{i,t-1}=0, this gives a_{i,t} in {0,1}. But a_{i,t}>0, so a_{i,t}=1.

Case 2: t=1. Then a_{i,1}>0. If i<=n-1, then i+1<=n, so i+1<=n implies i+1? More directly, with j=1, we have i+1<=n exactly when i<=n-1, and then i+1? Using hypothesis (i), since i+1<=n means i+1? equivalently i+1<=n, we get i+1? The relevant condition is i+1? No: hypothesis (i) says a_{i,1}=0 whenever i+1<=n, i.e. whenever i<=n-1. That would contradict a_{i,1}>0. Thus i=n. Now hypothesis (i) gives a_{n-1,1}=0 because (n-1)+1=n. Applying hypothesis (ii) at (n-1,1),
a_{n,1}-a_{n-1,1} is in {0,1}.
Since a_{n-1,1}=0, we get a_{n,1} in {0,1}. Because a_{n,1}=a_{i,t}>0, it follows that a_{i,t}=1.

So in all cases a_{i,t}=1.

Finally, for each k=t,t+1,...,j-1, hypothesis (iii) gives a_{i,k+1}-a_{i,k} in {0,1}. Summing these differences,
a_{i,j} = a_{i,t} + sum_{k=t}^{j-1} (a_{i,k+1}-a_{i,k})
<= 1 + (j-t)
= j-t+1
= x_{i,j}.
Thus a_{i,j}<=x_{i,j}, as required.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix integers n >= 2 and a matrix A = [a_{i,j}] satisfying the three stated conditions. Let i,j be such that 1 <= i,j <= n and a_{i,j} > 0. Define

y_{i,j} = #{k in {1,...,i} : a_{k,j} > 0}.

We must prove a_{i,j} <= y_{i,j}.

Let

r := min{k in {1,...,i} : a_{k,j} > 0}.

This minimum exists because a_{i,j} > 0.

First note that condition (ii) implies the entries in each fixed column are nondecreasing downwards: for every t with 1 <= t <= n-1,

a_{t+1,j} - a_{t,j} in {0,1},

so a_{t+1,j} >= a_{t,j}. Hence for every k with r <= k <= i we have a_{k,j} >= a_{r,j} > 0. By the minimality of r, for every k < r we have a_{k,j} = 0. Therefore the positive entries among a_{1,j},...,a_{i,j} are exactly those with indices r,r+1,...,i, and so

y_{i,j} = i-r+1.

It remains to show a_{i,j} <= i-r+1.

Case 1: r > 1.

Then a_{r-1,j} = 0 by the definition of r. Applying condition (ii) at row r-1 gives

a_{r,j} in {a_{r-1,j}, a_{r-1,j}+1} = {0,1}.

Since a_{r,j} > 0, it follows that a_{r,j} = 1.

Now for each t = r,r+1,...,i-1, condition (ii) gives

a_{t+1,j} - a_{t,j} <= 1.

Summing these inequalities from t=r to t=i-1, we obtain

a_{i,j} - a_{r,j} <= i-r.

Using a_{r,j} = 1, this yields

a_{i,j} <= 1 + (i-r) = i-r+1 = y_{i,j}.

Case 2: r = 1.

Then a_{1,j} > 0. By condition (i), if j <= n-1 then 1+j <= n, which would force a_{1,j} = 0, contradiction. Hence j = n.

Now condition (i) gives a_{1,n-1} = 0 because 1 + (n-1) = n. Applying condition (iii) at (1,n-1), we get

a_{1,n} in {a_{1,n-1}, a_{1,n-1}+1} = {0,1}.

Since a_{1,n} > 0, we conclude a_{1,n} = 1.

Applying condition (ii) down column n, for each t = 1,2,...,i-1 we have

a_{t+1,n} - a_{t,n} <= 1.

Summing from t=1 to t=i-1 gives

a_{i,n} - a_{1,n} <= i-1.

Using a_{1,n} = 1, we obtain

a_{i,n} <= 1 + (i-1) = i.

Since r=1, all entries a_{1,n},...,a_{i,n} are positive, so y_{i,n} = i. Thus again

a_{i,j} = a_{i,n} <= i = y_{i,n}.

In both cases, a_{i,j} <= y_{i,j}. Since i,j were arbitrary subject to a_{i,j} > 0, the claim holds for every such pair.

lemmas.proof_nl:
We prove the claim by strong induction on the integer t=i+j.

For each t with 2<=t<=2n, let Q(t) be the statement:
for every pair (i,j) with 1<=i,j<=n and i+j=t, one has a_{i,j}<=max(0,t-n).

Base case: t<=n.
If i+j=t<=n, then hypothesis (i) gives a_{i,j}=0. Hence
a_{i,j}=0=max(0,t-n).
So Q(t) holds for every t<=n.

Inductive step: fix t with n<t<=2n, and assume Q(s) holds for every s<t. We must prove Q(t).
Take any (i,j) with 1<=i,j<=n and i+j=t.

Because t>n>=2, we cannot have i=j=1, so at least one of i>1 or j>1 holds.

Case 1: i>1.
Then 1<=i-1<=n-1, so hypothesis (ii) applied to (i-1,j) yields
a_{i,j}-a_{i-1,j} in {0,1}.
Therefore a_{i,j}<=a_{i-1,j}+1.
Now (i-1)+j=t-1<t, so by the induction hypothesis Q(t-1),
a_{i-1,j}<=max(0,(t-1)-n).
Since t>n and t is an integer, t>=n+1, hence (t-1)-n>=0. Thus
max(0,(t-1)-n)=t-1-n.
So
a_{i,j}<=a_{i-1,j}+1<= (t-1-n)+1=t-n=max(0,t-n).

Case 2: i=1.
Then j=t-1, and since t>n>=2 we have j>1. Hence 1<=j-1<=n-1, so hypothesis (iii) applied to (1,j-1) yields
a_{1,j}-a_{1,j-1} in {0,1}.
Therefore a_{1,j}<=a_{1,j-1}+1.
Also 1+(j-1)=t-1<t, so by Q(t-1),
a_{1,j-1}<=max(0,(t-1)-n)=t-1-n,
again because t>n. Hence
a_{1,j}<=a_{1,j-1}+1<= (t-1-n)+1=t-n=max(0,t-n).

In both cases, every entry with i+j=t satisfies a_{i,j}<=max(0,t-n). Thus Q(t) holds.

By strong induction, Q(t) holds for all t from 2 to 2n. Therefore for every 1<=i,j<=n,
a_{i,j}<=max(0,i+j-n).
This is exactly the desired conclusion.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix an integer n >= 1 and integers l_1,\dots,l_n with 0 <= l_1 <= \cdots <= l_n and l_i <= i for all i. Define
E = { (i,j) : 1 <= i,j <= n and n-l_i+1 <= j <= n }.
For each (i,j) in E, define
x_{i,j} = #{ k in {1,\dots,j} : (i,k) in E }.
We must prove
\sum_{(i,j)\in E} x_{i,j} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{l_i(l_i+1)}{2}.

For each fixed i in {1,\dots,n}, let
E_i = { j : (i,j) \in E }.
By the definition of E,
E_i = { j : n-l_i+1 <= j <= n }.
Hence E_i consists of exactly the last l_i columns of row i. In particular, if l_i=0 then E_i is empty, while if l_i>0 then
E_i = { n-l_i+1, n-l_i+2, \dots, n }.
Therefore
\sum_{(i,j)\in E} x_{i,j} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j\in E_i} x_{i,j}.
So it is enough to compute the inner sum for each fixed i.

Fix i. Take any j \in E_i. Since (i,k) \in E exactly when k \in E_i, we have
x_{i,j} = #{ k in {1,\dots,j} : k \in E_i }.
Now E_i = { n-l_i+1, \dots, n }, so among the integers 1,\dots,j, the members of E_i are precisely
n-l_i+1, n-l_i+2, \dots, j.
Thus
x_{i,j} = j-(n-l_i+1)+1 = j-n+l_i.

It is convenient to reindex the elements of E_i. Write
j = n-l_i+t,
where t runs from 1 to l_i. Then the above formula gives
x_{i,j} = (n-l_i+t)-n+l_i = t.
Hence, for this fixed i,
\sum_{j\in E_i} x_{i,j} = \sum_{t=1}^{l_i} t = \frac{l_i(l_i+1)}{2}.
This also holds when l_i=0, since then both sides are 0.

Summing over i=1,\dots,n, we obtain
\sum_{(i,j)\in E} x_{i,j}
= \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j\in E_i} x_{i,j}
= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{l_i(l_i+1)}{2}.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

For each k = 1,...,n let mu_k be the number of indices i in {1,...,n} with l_i >= k. For each (i,j) in E let y_{i,j} be the number of r in {1,...,i} such that (r,j) is also in E. lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix k in {1,...,n}, and let j_k := n-k+1. Then j_k is a column index in {1,...,n}, and as k runs from 1 to n, the numbers j_k run through all columns exactly once.

For any row index i, we have
(i,j_k) in E
if and only if n-l_i+1 <= j_k <= n.
Since j_k = n-k+1, this is equivalent to
n-l_i+1 <= n-k+1,
that is, l_i >= k.
Hence the set of rows whose cell in column j_k belongs to E is exactly
I_k := { i in {1,...,n} : l_i >= k }.
By definition, |I_k| = mu_k.

Now list the elements of I_k in increasing order:
I_k = {i_1 < i_2 < ... < i_{mu_k}}
if mu_k > 0. For each t = 1,...,mu_k, consider the cell (i_t,j_k). By definition,
y_{i_t,j_k} = # { r in {1,...,i_t} : (r,j_k) is in E }.
But (r,j_k) is in E exactly when r is in I_k, so
 y_{i_t,j_k} = # { r <= i_t : r in I_k }.
Among the elements of I_k, exactly i_1,...,i_t are <= i_t. Therefore
 y_{i_t,j_k} = t.
So the total contribution from column j_k is
sum over all i with (i,j_k) in E of y_{i,j_k}
= sum_{t=1}^{mu_k} t
= mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.
If mu_k = 0, then the column contributes 0, which is again mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.

Finally, the columns j_k for k=1,...,n are precisely all columns of the n by n grid, so E is the disjoint union over k=1,...,n of the cells in column j_k. Therefore
sum_{(i,j) in E} y_{i,j}
= sum_{k=1}^n sum over all i with (i,j_k) in E of y_{i,j_k}
= sum_{k=1}^n mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix an integer n >= 1 and integers 0 <= l_1 <= l_2 <= ... <= l_n <= n. For each k in {1,...,n}, let
mu_k = #{ i in {1,...,n} : l_i >= k }.
We prove
sum_{k=1}^n mu_k(mu_k+1)/2 = sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)l_i.

Because each l_i is a nonnegative integer, we may write
(n+1-i)l_i = sum_{k=1}^{l_i} (n+1-i) = sum_{k=1}^n (n+1-i) * 1_{\{l_i >= k\}}.
Summing over i gives
sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)l_i
= sum_{i=1}^n sum_{k=1}^n (n+1-i) * 1_{\{l_i >= k\}}.
Since this is a finite double sum, we may interchange the order of summation:
sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)l_i
= sum_{k=1}^n sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i) * 1_{\{l_i >= k\}}
= sum_{k=1}^n sum_{i: l_i >= k} (n+1-i).

Now fix k in {1,...,n}. Since l_1 <= l_2 <= ... <= l_n, the set of indices i with l_i >= k is a terminal segment of {1,...,n}. Its cardinality is mu_k, so necessarily
{i : l_i >= k} = {n-mu_k+1, n-mu_k+2, ..., n}
(with the understanding that this set is empty when mu_k = 0). Therefore
sum_{i: l_i >= k} (n+1-i)
= sum_{i=n-mu_k+1}^n (n+1-i).
Putting r = n+1-i, as i runs from n-mu_k+1 to n, the value of r runs from mu_k down to 1. Hence
sum_{i=n-mu_k+1}^n (n+1-i) = sum_{r=1}^{mu_k} r = mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.
So for every k,
sum_{i: l_i >= k} (n+1-i) = mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.
Substituting into the previous expression yields
sum_{i=1}^n (n+1-i)l_i = sum_{k=1}^n mu_k(mu_k+1)/2.
This is exactly the claimed identity.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Let
\[
T:=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(i+j-n).
\]
For each fixed row index \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), the points of \(E\) in that row are exactly
\[
(i,j)\quad\text{with}\quad n-l_i+1\le j\le n.
\]
Hence, if we write
\[
T_i:=\sum_{j=n-l_i+1}^{n}(i+j-n),
\]
with the usual convention that this is the empty sum when \(l_i=0\), then the rows are disjoint and cover \(E\), so
\[
T=\sum_{i=1}^n T_i.
\]
It therefore suffices to compute each \(T_i\).

Fix \(i\). We consider two cases.

If \(l_i=0\), then there is no integer \(j\) with \(n-l_i+1=n+1\le j\le n\), so \(T_i=0\). Also
\[
\frac{l_i(2i-l_i+1)}2=\frac{0(2i-0+1)}2=0.
\]
Thus in this case
\[
T_i=\frac{l_i(2i-l_i+1)}2.
\]

Now assume \(l_i\ge 1\). Then the allowed values of \(j\) are
\[
j=n-l_i+1,\,n-l_i+2,\,\dots,\,n.
\]
Set
\[
j=n-l_i+t\qquad (t=1,2,\dots,l_i).
\]
This reindexes the sum bijectively, so
\[
T_i=\sum_{t=1}^{l_i}\bigl(i+(n-l_i+t)-n\bigr)
=\sum_{t=1}^{l_i}(i-l_i+t).
\]
Therefore
\[
T_i=\sum_{t=1}^{l_i}(i-l_i)+\sum_{t=1}^{l_i}t
=l_i(i-l_i)+\frac{l_i(l_i+1)}2.
\]
Simplifying,
\[
T_i=\frac{2l_i(i-l_i)+l_i(l_i+1)}2
=\frac{2il_i-l_i^2+l_i}{2}
=\frac{l_i(2i-l_i+1)}2.
\]
So this formula also holds when \(l_i\ge 1\).

Thus for every \(i=1,\dots,n\),
\[
T_i=\frac{l_i(2i-l_i+1)}2.
\]
Summing over \(i\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(i+j-n)
=T
=\sum_{i=1}^n T_i
=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{l_i(2i-l_i+1)}2.
\]
This is exactly the claimed identity.
